client: I've been really struggling lately with this anxiety about my final exams coming up, and honestly it's been keeping me up at night. I got a low grade on my last psychology paper and now I can't stop thinking that I'm going to fail everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still going to happen whether I feel better about them or not.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of worry right now, and that one low grade has really snowballed into a fear that everything might fall apart — that kind of spiral can make sleep and focus feel almost impossible. I also hear your skepticism about whether talking helps, and that's actually a really honest and important thing to name; what we *can* work on here isn't making the exams disappear, but loosening the grip that anxious thinking has on you so you can actually access what you know. When you say you're going to "fail everything," what specific thoughts tend to run through your mind when that fear hits hardest?

client: Honestly, when the fear hits hardest, it's usually something like "you're not smart enough to be here" or "everyone else gets this except you." And then it just kind of cascades into this image of me having to call my parents and tell them I'm failing out, and seeing the disappointment on their faces. I know it sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely real and inevitable.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — those thoughts and that image of your parents' disappointment feel very real and painful, and it makes complete sense that your mind goes there when you're under this much pressure. What you're describing are classic examples of what we call cognitive distortions — "I'm not smart enough" and "everyone else gets it" are actually predictions and comparisons your anxious mind is presenting as facts. I'm curious: if you look at the actual evidence in your life, what are some things that suggest you *do* belong there, even if they feel small right now?

client: I mean... I did get accepted into the program, and they don't just let anyone in, I guess. But it's hard to hold onto that when I'm sitting in a seminar and someone asks a question I never even thought of, and it just feels like proof that I don't belong there. It's like my brain immediately grabs onto the bad stuff and the good stuff just kind of slides off.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence that challenges the "I don't belong" story, even if it's hard to hold onto right now. What you're describing, where your brain latches onto the negative moments and lets the positive ones slip away, is actually a well-known pattern called a negativity bias, and it's something we can actively work against. I'm wondering, what would it look like to intentionally "collect" small pieces of evidence over the next few days that you *do* belong — almost like building a case for the defense?

client: I get what you're saying, and the idea of "building a case" actually makes some sense to me intellectually. But I guess my worry is that in the moment, when I'm sitting alone at lunch or nobody's texting back, those small positive things just feel so... irrelevant, you know? Like, how do I hold onto them when the loneliness is right there in my face?
therapist: There's something really tender in what you're sharing — it sounds like underneath the exam anxiety, there's also a loneliness that makes those harder moments feel even heavier and harder to escape. You're right that intellectual understanding doesn't always reach us when we're in the middle of a painful feeling, and that gap between "knowing" and "feeling" is actually one of the most human things about this work. I'm wondering, when you're sitting alone at lunch and that loneliness hits, what does the story your mind tells you in that moment actually sound like?

client: It's like my mind just goes straight to "nobody here actually wants to talk to you" or "you're the kind of person people tolerate but don't actually seek out." And then I start replaying little moments from earlier in the day, like if someone walked past me without saying hi, and I build this whole case against myself. It's exhausting because I know logically that people are just busy, but in that moment the evidence feels so real and damning.
therapist: What strikes me is that you're actually already doing the "building a case" work — just against yourself, using the same selective evidence we talked about earlier, like that person walking past without saying hi. It's exhausting to be your own harshest prosecutor, and it makes sense your mind does this, but it's worth noticing that you're applying a very different standard to yourself than you would to, say, a friend in the same situation. If a close friend told you "nobody here actually wants to talk to me," what evidence would *you* point them toward, and how would your voice sound different from the one in your own head?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, if a friend said that to me I'd probably point out all the times people did make an effort to include them, or remind them that one person walking by doesn't mean everyone hates them. But when it's me, that logic just doesn't seem to stick the same way — it feels different from the inside, like I actually know the truth about myself and I'm not just being paranoid. I guess I'm not sure how to make my own brain believe the kinder version the way I'd believe it for someone else.
therapist: What you just said is really insightful — you noticed exactly the double standard, and yet there's this deeply held sense that when it comes to *you*, the harsh version is just "the truth" rather than a thought that could be questioned. That feeling of "I actually know the real me" is one of the trickiest parts of this kind of thinking, because it disguises itself as self-awareness rather than self-criticism. I'm curious — where do you think that voice learned to be so much harder on you than you would ever be on someone you care about?

client: I've been sitting with that question and... I think it started at home, honestly. My parents weren't cruel or anything, but there was this constant undercurrent of "you could do better, you should try harder," and I internalized that as just being realistic about myself. It's weird to think of it as a voice that "learned" something rather than just... the truth, because it still feels so true when it speaks up.
therapist: That's a really meaningful thing to recognize — that what feels like "just being realistic" was actually a message you absorbed over years from people you loved and needed, and it makes complete sense it feels like truth rather than a learned story. The fact that it came from a place of love, not cruelty, can actually make it harder to question, because part of you may feel like challenging it means criticizing your parents or rejecting something that "helped" you get this far. I'm wondering, do you think there's a difference between the drive to do well that helped you get into this program, and the voice that tells you you're never quite enough — and what would it feel like to keep one without the other?

client: That's... actually a really hard question to sit with, because part of me wants to say yes, they're different things, but when I try to actually separate them in my head, they feel completely tangled together. Like, what if the drive only works because of the fear underneath it — what if I take away the "you're never enough" voice and I just stop trying altogether? I guess I'm scared that the anxiety is the engine, and without it I'd just fall apart.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense, and it's actually one of the most common things people discover when they start to question their inner critic — this worry that the harsh voice is the only thing holding them together. But I'd gently invite you to consider: the evidence suggests your drive has produced real things, like getting into a competitive program, pushing through hard papers, showing up even when it's painful — and those came from *you*, not just from fear. What if the anxiety has been a passenger claiming to be the driver all along, and there's something steadier underneath it that's actually been doing the work?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard not to feel like the anxiety and the drive are just... the same thing. Like, if I take away the fear of failing or disappointing everyone, I genuinely don't know what would be left to push me forward. What if I stopped worrying and just became complacent, and then everything I've worked for falls apart?
therapist: There's a real vulnerability in what you're sharing — like you're standing at the edge of something and not sure the ground will hold if you let go of what's familiar, even when it hurts. It's worth gently noticing though that complacency and relief aren't the same thing — people can be motivated by curiosity, by genuine care about their future, by pride in their work, and those are quieter but much more sustainable engines than fear. I'm curious: can you think of even one moment in your studies where you felt pulled toward something rather than pushed by anxiety — where interest or satisfaction, not fear, was what kept you going?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, it's always been fear. But... there was this one time last semester when I got really absorbed in a paper I was writing about social psychology, and I stayed up late not because a deadline was looming but because I genuinely wanted to figure out what I was trying to say. I almost don't trust that memory though, because I can't tell if I'm just telling myself a nicer story about it now.
therapist: That memory is really significant, and I don't think you're making it up — the fact that it feels unfamiliar and slightly untrustworthy might actually be evidence that it's real, because your mind isn't used to counting those moments as meaningful data about yourself. You stayed up late chasing an idea, not running from a deadline, and that's a completely different relationship with your own thinking than the one the anxious voice describes. I'm wondering, what was it about that social psychology topic that pulled you in — what were you trying to figure out?
